newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin calls for action on Russian wage delays.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin calls for action on Russian wage delays.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin cracked the whip on Tuesday, outlining key economic tasks for his new-look cabinet and accusing Russia's conservative parliament of shoddy work on preparing laws.
Yeltsin met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the Kremlin and urged him, not for the first time, to improve tax collection and tackle chronic delays in paying state sector wages.
"The first thing, of course, is salaries, and certainly another issue is tax collection," Yeltsin said at the start of the meeting, which was broadcast on Russian Public Television.
The Kremlin leader also told Chernomyrdin to prepare a presidential report with guidelines for Russia's 1998 budget by April 20 and speed up a long-awaited new tax code.
The rest of the meeting was held behind closed doors.

Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky made clear that the Kremlin leader, who has been putting the final touches to the reshuffled cabinet, would focus on economic reform rather than personnel changes in his talks with Chernomyrdin.
Yeltsin also rebuked the speaker of the Duma, the communist-dominated lower house of parliament.
"The high level of political tensions in the State Duma has reduced the effectiveness of the chamber's legislative work," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling speaker Gennady Seleznyov.
Yeltsin said he had been forced to return up to 75 percent of legislative acts to the Duma because they were poorly prepared.

Alarmed by growing public discontent over chronic wage and pension delays and a web of non-payments strangling the economy, Yeltsin dramatically reshuffled his cabinet in March, reinforcing it with young, reform-oriented ministers.

Yeltsin and his reformist first deputy prime ministers, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, have announced overhauls of the financial sector and welfare programmes. But so far they have been preoccupied shaping the new government.
The Kremlin leader has still to decide the future of the heads of the energy ministry and the tax agency, who have tendered their resignations.
The new-look government underwent its first test on March 27 when trade unions ran nationwide protests demanding an end to wage delays which can stretch back more than six months.

Economists say the wage delays, which have cost Yeltsin and his government a dangerous drop in popularity, were caused by companies failing to pay each other and the government collecting insufficient taxes to cover its spending.
The tax collection crisis has forced the government and parliamentary officials to consider changes in the 1997 budget to cut spending for the remainder of the year.

Government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said a top minister would brief the Duma on the financial results of the first quarter on April 23. Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying that spending cuts may also be raised on that day.

The government insists that the problem cannot be overcome without radical cuts in state support for loss-making state-run enterprises and painful reforms in the welfare system, one of the last vestiges of the paternalistic communist state.

But it says such reforms -- in a country whose economy is dominated by uncompetitive enterprises and whose people live on an average monthly income of less than $200 -- should be extra-cautious to avoid a social explosion.
Yeltsin's press office said Yeltsin would on Wednesday meet at least 10 regional leaders, whose backing is badly needed to help boost reform and soften its possible negative consequences.
